In the printed tradition, are the accents of the Decalogue grammatical?

The question

The two Decalogues (Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5) are each chanted two ways: the טעם תחתון (taḥton, “lower”) division into ordinary-length verses, and the טעם עליון (elyon, “upper”) division by commandment, which makes the short prohibitions (לא תרצח, לא תנאף, לא תגנב) their own tiny verses and folds long passages into single long ones. Issue #36 grammar-checked the Tiberian-manuscript (WLC / MAM) taḥton and elyon threads by detangling WLC’s dual cantillation. This page (issue #52) asks the companion question for the printed editions (דפוסים, also Koren and Simanim): fed through the very same prose grammar checker, are their taḥton and elyon accentuations grammatical too?

Unlike the manuscript thread, the printed and manuscript readings are already single cantillation, spelled out word-for-word on the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים. Each chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is fed through the shared pipeline — a leading verse-start token, the prose scanner, then the prose PLY grammar — exactly as issue #36 does. The manuscript versions are the baseline (MAM’s own authoritative text, expected all clean); the printed versions are the object of study.

The verdict

Tiberian manuscriptPrinted editions
Exodus 20 — taḥton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Exodus 20 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deuteronomy 5 — taḥton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deuteronomy 5 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

taḥton is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. The printed taḥton differs from the manuscript only in details that do not touch the accent grammar (vocalization such as תִּרְצַח vs תִּרְצָח at לא תרצח, and where a maqaf or ga‘ya falls), and in one verse boundary: the printed taḥton ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the manuscript, which runs the first two commandments together). Both parse clean.

elyon is grammatical in the manuscript but not in the printed editions: the printed elyon of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

Why the printed elyon fails: the merged first verse

In the manuscript elyon, the first commandment אָנֹכִי … עֲבָדִים is its own chanted verse, and לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The printed editions instead merge the first two commandments into a single verse (nine chanted verses in all, against the manuscript’s ten). That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects. Shown accent-stripped and divided at the printed taḥton’s verse boundaries — one elyon verse (E) spanning the five ordinary taḥton verses (T) it merges:

Eאָֽנֹכִי…מִצְוֺתָֽי׃
Tאָֽנֹכִי…עֲבָדִֽים׃לֹֽא־יִהְיֶה…עַל־פָּנָֽי׃לֹֽא־תַעֲשֶׂה…לָאָֽרֶץ׃לֹֽא־תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה…לְשֹׂנְאָֽי׃וְעֹשֶׂה…מִצְוֺתָֽי׃
e
t

The single etnaḥta falls at לְשֹׂנְאָי, leaving an over-long first half that carries a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עֲבָדִים, עַל־פָּנַי, and לָאָרֶץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy’s printed elyon Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the manuscript’s two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.

Source

All eight readings (two books × taḥton/elyon × manuscript/printed) are taken from the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים (revision 2810844, 2023-10-22), which every printed-vs-manuscript comparison table there transcludes. A handful of wiki templates are resolved to plain pointed text (legarmeh/paseq to a paseq mark, qere for ketiv-qere, paragraph and pisqa markers dropped); the chanted verses are split at sof pasuq.
